editor_spans.body: Burnham's case contradicts itself. His best example of power held close to the ground is Easterhouse. He says he went there 'with the help of the ground-breaking Scottish Violence Reduction Unit', which is a national Scottish body. The project ran under the same Holyrood system he now calls 'one of the most centralised nations in Europe'. So the model he wants to roll out 'nationwide' came out of the structure he says is holding Scotland back. The lesson he takes from it is about scale: Westminster should pay to take a local charity's approach to the whole country. That is just as much a top-down plan as the ones he criticises. A model he praises as 'run by the local community and the people on the estate' would be rolled out by two governments.

The offer is not equal between the two governments. What Westminster can give comes from reserved budgets: DWP employment support and innovation money, taken from a £1 billion pot shared across the whole UK. The 'regional' tier he describes would need Holyrood to create new bodies or hand over its own powers to them. Scotland has no mayors. The only existing structures are the City Region Deals, and the Scottish Government's own reform of local government is already under way, which Burnham says is too slow. Calling this 'two governments working together' hides that it asks much more of Holyrood than of Westminster. This fits the argument I made last week (S354): the language of cooperation is also a way to compete with the SNP on its own ground, now with a date set by the National Economic Council meeting.

There is a gap in the history he tells. Ravenscraig and the Leigh pits were closed by national decisions about steel and coal. He describes them as decisions 'taken hundreds of miles away'. But regional control over employability and research funding would not have stopped either closure. The things that would have helped are mainly the ones that stay at UK level: buying British through public procurement, the EU food and farming deal, shipbuilding, and Grangemouth. The speech puts devolution first, but the strongest example of reindustrialisation in it is the buses he ordered from Alexander Dennis in Falkirk. That was a decision about what to buy, not about who holds power. Whether Scotland is reindustrialised will depend more on the UK procurement rules he promises than on whatever regional model comes out of the talks.

  S354 (the Editor's): Read together, three announcements from one week show a single political strategy: Great British Railways' headquarters going to Derby, the 'No10 North' offer to Holyrood, and the apprenticeship pledges. Each moves institutions and decisions away from London. The Scotland offer goes further. It turns Westminster's devolution argument against the Scottish Government, calling it 'one of the most centralised devolved administrations in Europe.' That gives the Prime Minister a way to compete with Holyrood on its own ground while appearing to offer cooperation.
  · The timing for the railway is worth noting. Building at Becketwell starts in early 2027 and is due to finish by spring 2029. That is close to the latest date for the next general election, so the building meant to embody public ownership may only just be ready before voters judge it. Until then, the claimed benefits depend on things a minister can announce, such as a fare freeze and extra seats, rather than an organisation that already exists. The headline 600 apprenticeships are also spread over four years and sit within a much bigger youth employment scheme.
